newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan court may rule on controversial law.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan court may rule on controversial law.

text.p: The chief justice of Pakistan's Supreme Court said on Tuesday that it was time the court decided whether the president should have the constitutional power to dissolve parliament and dismiss an elected government.
Sajjad Ali Shah's comments follow last month's dissolution of parliament by President Farooq Leghari, who also sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.

"We can go into it and give a decision whether it is going to stay or not," the chief justice said of the Eighth Amendment, which Leghari used to dissolve parliament. "Why should we postpone it again and again?"
He was speaking as the Supreme Court was hearing a petition filed by National Assembly Speaker Yousaf Raza Gilani against the president's dissolution of the assembly on November 5.
The controversial amendment, inserted into the constitution by former military ruler General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq in 1985, has been used by three presidents to dissolve four assemblies.
Leghari, once a close political ally of Bhutto, vowed when he became president in 1993 never to use his powers to dismiss an elected government, and now says he used them reluctantly.

Both major political parties, Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party and Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League, say they oppose the Eighth Amendment but have never joined forces to gain the two-thirds parliamentary majority required to quash it.
Bhutto has also filed a petition with the Supreme Court asking it to overturn her dismissal and restore the assembly.
After removing her government, Leghari installed a caretaker cabinet under Prime Minister Meraj Khalid to supervise fresh national and provincial assembly elections on February 3.
It was not immediately clear if the Supreme Court had the power to strike down part of the constitution.
